articles.title: EU nationals will pay higher tuition fees than UK students, Burnham indicates
articles.text:
European students will have to pay higher fees than their domestic equivalents at UK universities under a still-to-be-finalised part of the new deal with the EU, Andy Burnham has indicated.
The issue of fees paid by EU nationals studying at British universities is the main element of the arrangement hailed by Burnham in Brussels on Friday that has not been agreed, with both sides giving an extra six months to reach a solution.
Since Brexit, EU students – aside from Irish nationals and those with settled status in the UK – are treated as overseas entrants, so pay tuition fees which can exceed £30,000 a year, rather than a home student rate capped at £9,790.
The EU has been pushing for a lower rate, as part of the reset deal agreed at Friday’s summit in Brussels, which also included plans for looser checks on food and drink, emissions trading and a mutual exchange scheme for young people.
There have also been reports that Brussels has pushed for EU students to pay the domestic rate, while an annual charge of about £12,000 was suggested as a possible compromise.
Asked by Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions to rule out an equal rate between UK and EU students, Burnham indicated that this was requested by the EU but it would not be granted.
“In relation to the deal, the right honourable lady is referring to the European negotiating position, which is not the British negotiating position,” he told her. “That has not been put on the table, and it will not be put on the table.”
Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “Both sides have agreed to negotiate a reciprocal agreement, and any deal would have to be in our national interest.”
Higher overseas fees are an important source of income for most UK universities, and dropping them significantly for EU students could cost the sector hundreds of millions of pounds a year.
Burnham said the deal on tuition fees with the EU was “not done” when asked by the leader of the opposition if the government would compensate universities.
He reiterated the UK’s position that the implementation of the deals agreed on Friday would not be dependent on an agreement about tuition fees, something EU officials took a different view of on Friday.
Burnham said Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, referred to the tuition fees talks as being “a separate piece of paper” to the main deal at the summit, meaning they were not linked.
He also said the Conservative party had to be clear on whether it opposed the plans: “Will it stand against a deal that will remove mountains of paperwork from British businesses and British exporters? A deal that the vast majority of Britain’s major supermarkets support because, they say, it can bring down pressure on the weekly shop? The Conservatives were once the party that opposed the imposition of red tape; they are now the red tape Tories.”

headlines: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
Poland says Russia tried to assassinate Ukrainian rapper twice

articles.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
articles.text:
Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
- Published
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.
Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.
Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.
Russia's embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.
In a statement, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".
Russian state media cite the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".
In a statement on Saturday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services.
"This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable," she said, adding that "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real."
The rapper's real name is Albert Vasiliev.
PET said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.
PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.
Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.
Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.
In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.
In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.
Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.
He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Copenhagen was already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians could still get a Schengen visa in another country and travel to Denmark.
Copenhagen wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

articles.title: Poland says Russia tried to assassinate Ukrainian rapper twice
articles.text:
Poland says Russia tried to assassinate Ukrainian rapper twice
Polish confirmation comes after Copenhagen reveals alleged Russian plot to kill US-Ukrainian citizen on Danish soil.
Polish authorities have said Russian intelligence services tried to kill a Ukrainian-American rapper visiting the country in August, after Copenhagen said Moscow had allegedly targeted the same man on Danish soil.
The alleged assassination plan targeted Albert Vasiliev, a rapper who performs under the name Kyivstoner and holds Ukrainian and US citizenship, according to Danish media.
Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Maciej Wewior confirmed the alleged plot to kill Vasiliev in Poland to The Associated Press news agency on Sunday.
On Friday, in response to Denmark’s statement about the alleged assassination plan, Poland’s Foreign Ministry had written, “It is the second assassination attempt against the same person. The first one was foiled on the Polish territory in August 2026.”
It also said that a Russian national had been arrested.
Polish authorities detained the suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Moscow, on August 7.
Denmark announced the expulsion of a Russian diplomat on Friday after it accused Moscow intelligence of plotting the assassination during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb in September.
Denmark’s intelligence agency, PET, said on the same day that it suspected Russia of planning the assassination with the help of a banned Danish gang.
Two Danish men appeared in court near Copenhagen on Friday, charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and attempted murder.
Russia dismissed the allegations through its embassy in Copenhagen, saying they were unsubstantiated.
Previously, on August 13, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk disclosed that a plot to kill a Ukrainian-American in Warsaw was thwarted. He did not disclose Vasiliev’s name at the time but said the target “was uncomfortable” for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s government.
Support for Ukraine
Vasiliev has expressed his support for Ukraine amid Russia’s ongoing war on the country and was performing across Europe this year before his concerts were cancelled for security reasons.
Russia’s domestic security service, the FSB, accused Vasiliev of being involved in supplying drones for an alleged Ukrainian attack on a defence enterprise in the Moscow region. It said he was “acting under the patronage” of Ukraine’s internal security service, the SBU.
Danish broadcaster DR reported that Vasiliev denied the FSB accusations.
Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Lokke Rasmussen told reporters on Friday that Denmark was also considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians.
Poland’s Foreign Ministry said it backed the move.
“Poland supports measures Denmark suggested to limit the access and freedom of travel of Russian nationals on the EU territory,” it said on X.
Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of staging dozens of attacks and other incidents across Europe since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russia has denied those accusations.

headlines: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court

articles.title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
articles.text:
Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.
It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.
The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.
The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.
The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.
The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.
Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.
Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”
In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”
In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”
He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.
Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.
In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.
It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.
The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.
The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.
Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.
On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

articles.title: US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court
articles.text:
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel.
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement.
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

headlines: US intelligence chief says he trusts Trump’s description of Putin as ‘my friend’
US intelligence chief defends Trump’s comments calling Putin his ‘friend’

articles.title: US intelligence chief says he trusts Trump’s description of Putin as ‘my friend’
articles.text:
Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Donald Trump “completely” after the US president called Vladimir Putin “a friend” during their recent meeting in China.
Clayton made the remarks on Sunday, where he was pressed during media appearances on Trump’s warm characterization of the Russian president – who is viewed as a chief US adversary – following his trilateral summit with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. After a backlash at home and aboard, Trump doubled down on Saturday and posted a photo of himself and Putin shaking hands with the caption “My Friend.”
On CNN’s State of the Union, Dana Bash asked Clayton whether he also thinks Putin is a friend to the US.
“The president is the greatest conductor of foreign policy in a very challenging time that we have seen,” said Clayton on Sunday. “Getting the three nuclear powers together and getting them to agree that they are not going to escalate, that they are going to communicate, that is historic. That is remarkable and, in that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely.”
Bash pressed on whether Clayton personally agrees that Putin should be considered a friend.
“Dana, in different contexts, you can use different words. The president pulling off that summit, getting the three of them together, is just remarkable,” Clayton replied.
Speaking with ABC’s Jonathan Karl on This Week, Clayton made similar comments, saying that “using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate” in the context of the summit.
“That conversation, that picture – historic, historic picture – was in the context of the three nuclear powers, the three main nuclear powers, getting together and saying, ‘We cannot have a nuclear incident,’” Clayton said on Sunday, referring to Trump’s post. “In that circle of that conversation, using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate.”
Clayton also dodged when asked again whether he thinks Putin should be considered a friend to the United States.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton responded.
Last week, Trump sidestepped questions about his views on a friendship with Putin.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said in a press briefing. “I have fantastic relationships with Putin, that’s a very good thing.”
Trump’s characterization of Putin has sparked backlash from US lawmakers and officials abroad.
“Who is he? He’s the man who has abducted tens of thousands of children, killed tens of thousands of civilians, targeted civilian infrastructure across Ukraine, detained Americans wrongfully, and continues to do so daily,” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer posted on social media.
“Embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” Schumer added. “Senate Democrats will always stand with Ukraine and against Putin and autocratic dictators around the world.”
“It’s beyond me,” Senator Jeanne Shaheen said in an interview with MS NOW. “I don’t understand the president’s admiration and cozying up to Vladimir Putin, who is a war criminal.”
Trump’s comments also drew rebukes abroad, including from the deputy leader of the rightwing party Reform UK.
“It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake,” Richard Tice told Sky News. “He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”
Trump’s description of Putin as a friend also drew criticism from European allies of Ukraine. “Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be,” the Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said.
Separately, Clayton also faced questions about the recent spate of technology outages across the US and said Americans should expect more disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems.
“And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service,” Clayton said on CNN’s State of the Union program. “That is going to happen.”
- Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: US intelligence chief defends Trump’s comments calling Putin his ‘friend’
articles.text:
US intelligence chief defends Trump’s comments calling Putin his ‘friend’
US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton says Trump’s comments were ‘entirely appropriate’ in the context of the summit.
United States Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has faced pressure to justify President Donald Trump’s claims that his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin is a “friend”.
In an appearance on the ABC News show This Week, journalist Jonathan Karl pressed Clayton on Trump’s recent remarks.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? Because Trump said he couldn’t answer that question,” Karl asked.
Clayton responded by calling Trump’s meeting “historic” and his remarks “appropriate”, but the intelligence chief also clarified that the US has not taken Russia’s side when it comes to the country’s invasion of Ukraine.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton said.
The scrutiny follows a first-ever confirmed meeting between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on November 19.
The three world leaders had a roundtable on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in Shenzhen, China.
Throughout his presidency, Trump has repeatedly praised Putin. In August 2025, Trump hosted the Russian leader in Alaska for Putin’s first visit to the US in nearly a decade.
Upon reuniting with Putin at the Shenzhen conference, Trump offered him a warm, light-hearted greeting.
“Who is he?” Trump joked, first pointing to Putin, then striding across the room to shake his hand. “He’s my friend.”
Trump has since doubled down on his remarks, posting several images of their meeting on social media, one of which bore the caption, “My Friend”.
When a reporter asked whether Russia was a “friend to America” in a news briefing on Friday, Trump brushed aside the question.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said, proceeding to explain that he and Putin had grown close during an investigation into whether Russia had interfered in his favour during the 2016 US presidential election.
“I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. And to be honest, he was very nice about it,” Trump explained.
The US State Department has long been critical of Russia over allegations of human rights abuses, including the torture and imprisonment of political dissidents.
Washington has also supported Ukraine after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, providing billions in security assistance and weaponry.
Under Trump, however, that support has cooled, with the US president openly criticising his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for failing to cut a deal with Russia.
Such remarks have divided Republicans, with critics like outgoing US Representative Don Bacon accusing Trump of “playing footsie” with Putin.
“Traditionally, Republicans stood up to Russia and China,” Bacon said last week. “We stood for freedom, and we stood up for countries that shared our values. President Trump has been terrible on this, right here.”
But in his television appearances on Sunday, Clayton defended Trump’s remarks, describing the president’s statements of friendship as “entirely appropriate” for building a personal rapport with the Russian leader.
He also praised Trump for uniting some of the world’s biggest powers for a conversation about nuclear proliferation.
“It should be assuring that you have the three world nuclear powers getting together and saying: We’re not going to go in that direction,” Clayton told This Week.
While the trilateral meeting concluded with a statement about “reducing nuclear risks”, critics point out no firm commitments were made.
Also on Sunday, in an appearance on CNN, Clayton reiterated his support for Trump’s remarks.
“In that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely,” Clayton said.

headlines: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
Myanmar has been found guilty of genocide. Should Israel be worried? – podcast

articles.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
articles.text:
The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.
In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.
The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.
It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.
“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”
Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.
“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”
There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.
The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.
The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.
The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.
Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.
The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.
In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.
Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.
In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.
In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.
The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.
Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.
“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”
The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

articles.title: Myanmar has been found guilty of genocide. Should Israel be worried? – podcast
articles.text:
For seven years, Yasmin Ullah had been part of the delegation arguing that Myanmar had committed genocide – one of the gravest human rights crimes – against Rohingya Muslims.
The genocide has directly affected Yasmin and her family. Last week she was in court to hear the international court of justice’s landmark verdict against Myanmar. “I was really kind of pinching myself. It felt like we were all able to breathe again,” she tells Annie Kelly.
The verdict could have far-reaching consequences – especially for Israel, which is also facing a genocide case at the ICJ. The Guardian journalist Kaamil Ahmed explains how the case unfolded and what could happen next.

headlines: When you see smoke, run: Rohingya who escaped Myanmar’s genocide tell their stories
‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling

articles.title: When you see smoke, run: Rohingya who escaped Myanmar’s genocide tell their stories
articles.text:
Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.
In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.
What happened during the escape from Myanmar – a journey through forests and over hills and rivers while being battered by monsoon rains – was a key part of the ruling made this week in The Hague that Myanmar had carried out a genocide against the Rohingya.
The international court of justice (ICJ) said it was not enough to say they had faced ethnic cleansing when soldiers had also killed those trying to escape – Myanmar was trying to destroy the group as a people.
Stories of that violence in 2017, of organised mass killing, sexual attacks and the complete destruction of their villages, came with the refugees who arrived in neighbouring Bangladesh, eventually numbering more than 700,000 and settling in what has become the world’s largest refugee camp.
For months, they would arrive from places such as Tula Toli, where thousands were rounded up, killed and buried in mass graves. In other villages, men were captured and killed by the security forces.
Many survivors had escaped an attack on their own village, only to watch their relatives being killed in the villages where they had sought safety.
Almost a decade later, the majority of Rohingya who arrived in 2017 remain in the refugee camps, joining those who had already been there since the early 1990s, having escaped previous military operations and ever-increasing persecution.
The ICJ ruling has come at a particularly harsh time for Rohingya refugees, in a year in which hundreds have died at sea trying to escape the refugee camps, and in which countries such as Malaysia and India have spoken about returning the Rohingya to Myanmar.
Rohingya campaigners are hoping that this ruling will put an end to that.
Rohingya refugees still live in fragile shelters made of bamboo and tarpaulin sheets. They are denied the right to leave the camps, to work or to seek education.
Below are some of the stories from Rohingya who arrived in Bangladesh in 2017, having escaped Tula Toli and the surrounding area.
Momtaz and Dildar Begum
Sitting in the background, almost unnoticed as Momtaz Begum recollected how Myanmar forces had killed her husband and children and then raped her in front of her lone surviving child, was a woman who seemed to know every word of the story.
It was not because she had heard it before. Dildar Begum had experienced exactly the same violence as her sister had, in their village, Tula Toli.
In fact, they had for months believed each other dead until they discovered that they had both made it to Bangladesh and lived in different parts of the camp.
Each had only one surviving daughter, both of whom had similar scars along the back of their heads.
Anwara Begum
Twice previously Anwara Begum had lived as a refugee in Bangladesh. Once as a child in 1978 and then again in the early 1990s, as a young mother who lost her son to a respiratory disease during a rainy season spent in a flimsy tent.
When she was forced to return to Myanmar, though the persecution she fled there had not stopped, Anwara swore to herself that she would never become a refugee again.
She broke that oath when she saw the river by her village filled with bodies floating from Tula Toli.
Her husband first pulled from the river as many bodies as he could to bury and then they gathered some belongings and headed westwards to the River Naf – the border with Bangladesh.
To cross, she handed over all the gold she owned, equal to US $200 (£150), to a Bangladeshi boatman.
Nur Alam
Elderly people were not spared the Myanmar military’s attacks. Like so many others, Nur Alam had to be carried on the shoulders of his children on his journey to Bangladesh.
His 10-year-old grandson, Mamoon, held his hand. Once in the camp, they stuck to each other.
Alam’s arrival in Bangladesh was his fourth time being a refugee there. He was first expelled from Myanmar – known as Burma until 1989 – during military operations in the 1950s when Bangladesh was not yet an independent country.

articles.title: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling
articles.text:
There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.
For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.
Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”
Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.
“During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they said. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.
“Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”
In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.
They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.
“Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes.
She said, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”
The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.
Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.
The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it said meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.
The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.
There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.
With continuing violence against the Rohingya, the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.
But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.
“We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” says Salma.

headlines: Trump hosts third crypto gala for meme coin amid conflict of interest outcry
Trump to host private dinner for largest owners of his meme coin

articles.title: Trump hosts third crypto gala for meme coin amid conflict of interest outcry
articles.text:
Donald Trump is scheduled to headline his third cryptocurrency gala on Sunday night at his country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures.
The dinner, set to take place at the Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, will include meet-and-greets with Trump supporters including the boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, NBA champion Tristan Thompson and mentalist Lior Suchard, according to the event’s website.
The gala’s access and perks are divided by tiers for the 185 holders of $TRUMP, the president’s meme coin. A Trump fragrance, a poster, a “commemorative” ticket, and a “Trump watch” are reserved for 120 attendees. Meanwhile, the top 29 investors are invited to a VIP reception, and the top four will receive a “TRUMP 18K Gold Watch”.
Trump has hosted two similar galas since he took office last year, bringing a flurry of criticism as Democrats accuse Trump and his family of monetizing his brand through an array of equities and crypto ventures while in office.
After sweepingwins in the midterms, Democrats have vowed to investigate conflicts of interest involving Trump and his personal wealth during his presidency. They also say they plan to push for legislation that would ban activities such as the meme coin gala dinner.
“This dinner and scoring mechanism appear carefully constructed to increase investment in $TRUMP, allowing the President to abuse the power of his office to personally enrich himself, as he has throughout this term,” reads a letter sent by Adam Schiff and eight other US senators last month.
Since returning to the White House, Trump has made more than $1bn from his crypto businesses, according to financial disclosures released in June. Trump received more than $500m from his World Liberty Financial business selling new crypto products, and raked another $600m from sales of souvenir-type “meme” coins stamped with Trump’s face. Trump launched his $Trump meme coin days before his inauguration.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Interest in the $TRUMP coin dinner has plummeted, with contestants’ combined holdings dropping from $148m in May 2025 to $8.6m in this month’s gala.
More than half of the digital wallets publicly listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday’s dinner are tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they are linked to foreign nationals, according to an analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.
“Neither the President nor his family has ever engaged — or will ever engage — in conflicts of interest,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Reuters earlier this year. “President Trump proudly made the United States the crypto capital of the world through executive actions.“
The Trump family’s other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record lows. Together, outside investors in their five main crypto and crypto-linked projects have lost more than $5bn, according to a Reuters analysis.
The Trump meme coin has earned the Trump family at least $635m, according to the president’s June financial disclosure statement. In total, the Trumps had earned at least $2.3bn through April from their four main crypto ventures, including the meme coin.
The president’s stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about $430m.
Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: Trump to host private dinner for largest owners of his meme coin
articles.text:
Trump to host private dinner for largest owners of his meme coin
Sunday’s dinner is the third private event for top holders of the $Trump meme coin, launched shortly before his second inauguration.
United States President Donald Trump will host a third private dinner for top investors in his meme coin $TRUMP, reigniting questions about potential conflicts of interest with his cryptocurrency ventures.
Sunday’s gala will take place at the Trump National Golf Club outside Washington, DC.
According to the dinner’s official website, the top 185 meme-coin holders will be invited to a gala dinner, where guests will include businessman Kevin O’Leary and boxer Floyd Mayweather.
The top 29 holders, meanwhile, will be given special access to a VIP reception where Trump will reportedly be present.
“There will be no private meetings with The President. No gifts will be accepted,” the website said of the VIP reception.
The event has been billed as “a once-in-a-lifetime experience — an evening you will talk about forever”.
But Democrats have accused the Republican leader of leveraging his public office for profit in violation of federal law. They see such dinners as an opportunity for private interests to pay for access to the president.
“Trump is continuing to exploit the presidency for his personal gain,” Kendall Witmer, the deputy communications director for the Democratic National Committee, said in a statement.
In October, shortly after the gala was announced, eight Democratic senators issued an open letter promising to investigate any conflicts of interest such an event might raise.
“President Trump’s continued monetization of his name and likeness once again raises serious ethical concerns, necessitating this request for a robust inquiry into the President’s financial entanglements and personal profiteering,” the letter said.
The Democratic Party has since won majorities in both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm race, paving the way for possible inquiries and subpoenas when the new members are sworn in next year.
Trump’s White House has dismissed the criticism, calling the dinner a “private event, not a government function”. It has also emphasised that “there is no promise of official government action in exchange for attending”.
Trump has also argued that many of his assets are held in a trust while he is in office, though that trust is largely run by his family members.
The president is a stakeholder in cryptocurrency firms like World Liberty Financial, and has made promoting cryptocurrency a central part of his second term.
Under his leadership, the US Treasury established a reserve of digital currency assets, as part of Trump’s effort to make the US the “crypto capital of the world”.
Sunday’s gala is believed to be the third such dinner for top $Trump meme coin holders.
Meme coins trade on a popular likeness from the internet. Trump launched his on January 17, 2025, days before the start of his second term.
To encourage meme-coin purchases, Trump and his business partners held private events on May 22, 2025, and again on April 25, 2026, for top holders of the cryptocurrency.
The first was held at the same Trump golf club outside Washington, DC, and the second took place at Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s Florida resort.
The May 2025 dinner reportedly required a minimum of $55,000 in $Trump coins to attend.
At the time, Chinese crypto investor Justin Sun was declared the winner of a “contest” for who held the most $TRUMP coins. Sun held about $18m of the coin in 2025, as well as tokens from World Liberty Financial.
Earlier this year, Sun sued World Liberty Financial, saying it had frozen his access to the assets he owned with it, making it impossible for him to sell them.
Trump’s inauguration in January 2025 proved a major boost for his coin, pushing its value to $74.
The $Trump coin has since lost value. On the eve of the gala dinner, it is worth about $0.88.
According to financial disclosure forms released earlier this year, Trump earned more than $2.2bn in 2025, the first year of his second term.
Much of that wealth came from meme coins, tokens and other digital assets. Some $636m came from $Trump meme coin sales.

headlines: Pochettino’s nightmare start as Man U thrashed by Liverpool
Liverpool 4-0 Manchester United: Five key takeaways for Pochettino

articles.title: Pochettino’s nightmare start as Man U thrashed by Liverpool
articles.text:
Pochettino’s nightmare start as Man U thrashed by Liverpool
NewsFeed
Pochettino’s nightmare start as Man U thrashed by Liverpool
Mauricio Pochettino could hardly have made a worse start as Manchester United manager. Pochettino’s team were beaten 4-0 by fierce rivals Liverpool and remain in the Premier League relegation zone.
Published On 23 Nov 2026

articles.title: Liverpool 4-0 Manchester United: Five key takeaways for Pochettino
articles.text:
Liverpool 4-0 Manchester United: Five key takeaways for Pochettino
United suffer their worst result under a new manager in 100 years as Liverpool cruise past Mauricio Pochettino’s side.
If Mauricio Pochettino had any doubt about the size of the job in front of him at Manchester United, his players confirmed his worst fears within 13 minutes of his first game in charge – a 4-0 defeat at Liverpool.
As the home side surged into a two-goal lead in the opening exchanges at Anfield, with the away side reduced to 10 men, the sinking sensation for United – who are second bottom of the Premier League – immediately returned.
Any ‘new-manager bounce’, as feared by Reds manager Andoni Iraola, had no time to materialise with a rash challenge from Lenny Yoro on Alexander Isak leading to a straight red in the eighth minute.
The resulting free-kick was powered home by Dominik Szoboszlai, with Florian Wirtz thereafter converting a sharp attack in a flash – ending the match as a contest.
Pochettino slammed the decision to send off Yoro after the game, but there was a familiar feeling about the performance overall.
Al Jazeera Sport takes a look at five key takeaways as the opening salvo of the ninth manager since United’s last league title in 2013 fell apart – resulting in the worst start for a new manager of the club in 100 years.
Was the referee right to send off Manchester United’s Lenny Yoro?
Even though United have greater concerns, the answer was undoubtedly: no. The question for the referee, in sending off Yoro for denying a goalscoring opportunity, had four considerations: distance between the offence and the goal, general direction of the play, likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball, and location and number of defenders.
Of those guidelines, the most pertinent were the direction of play, which was at an angle across the box, and the likelihood of keeping control of the ball – Isak arguably had no control of it at all after a heavy first touch that allowed United keeper Senne Lammens to gather.
VAR (video assistant referee) had the chance to ask the referee to reconsider his decision, but decided there was no clear and obvious error. Had the referee reviewed the red card, then he would have surely decided a yellow card would have sufficed.
The play that led to the card being shown, however, was even more questionable than the outcome.
Was Pochettino right to bench Maguire for Man United?
The release of the team sheets, an hour and 15 minutes before kickoff, was the first moment all United fans looked to.
For all the pre-game comments by Pochettino, the Argentinean’s starting 11 was always going to be the first true sense of his evaluation of United’s current woes.
Dropping defender Harry Maguire, a former club captain, was a massive call – all the more so given the inexperience of Yoro and Matthijs de Ligt, who were both selected ahead of the ex-England stalwart.
The ref’s mistake in sending off Yoro was clear, but Yoro and de Ligt were heavily exposed in the play that led to the sending-off.
The latter is easing his way back into first-team action after a year out with a back injury and found himself in no-man’s land as Isak chased a long ball. Yoro sought to cover, but was clumsy and ill-advised in his attempt, allowing Isak to draw what was only a soft challenge and connection.
United were plucky after the change forced by the sending-off, with Maguire replacing the clearly, and understandably, disappointed Bryan Mbeumo.
Maguire’s fine, last-ditch block from Isak’s close-range pivot and shot saved United’s blushes five minutes before the break, and made Pochettino’s first big call look all the worse.
A scuffed attempt at a clearance early in the second half by de Ligt allowed Isak clean through only for the Liverpool forward to slice his effort.
By the time Rio Ngumoha added a 66th-minute third, all the questions about a defence that had previously shipped 30 goals in 15 games this season had been answered. The fourth from Victor Munoz was inevitable, and it could have been a lot worse for United on the day.
Their last defeat at Anfield was a 7-0 victory for the home side – a repeat was certainly possible had Liverpool been more clinical.
Matters were so bad that the former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher commented on Sky Sports that he “felt sorry” for de Ligt prior to his eventual substitution in the second half.
The consensus was that Pochettino made the wrong call before the start.
What other Man United changes did Pochettino make at Liverpool?
Yoro and de Ligt have been peripheral figures in their time with the Old Trafford club, for varying reasons including injury, but they were not the only big calls made by Pochettino.
Another injury-plagued player, Patrick Dorgu, was also given a start – and in a formation which was not wholly clear. The popular Amad Diallo was forced to make do with a place on the bench alongside Maguire.
Dorgu, whose form has been indifferent at best, can operate as a wide defender or attacker. It appeared as though he was given some licence on the left to get forward, with United reverting to a back four, Lisandro Martinez covering on the flank in defence and Diogo Dalot holding back on the right.
Whether it was a back four or five to begin with – the latter explaining the absence of the more forward-minded Diallo – United were quickly forced to a five with the sending-off and the sacrifice of Mbeumo at the other end of the pitch.
Not only was the decision to pick two less experienced centre-backs at Anfield a monumental – and ultimately costly – call, the move to switch to an unfamiliar feel across the backline was a painful lesson for Pochettino, who himself is more accustomed to a 4-2-3-1 setup.
What next for Manchester United and Mauricio Pochettino?
With 19th-placed United mired in the Premier League drop zone, the UEFA Champions League appears a sideshow, but a trip to Sporting Lisbon awaits on Wednesday.
In some ways, Europe’s elite club competition, which United have returned to after a three-year absence, may well give Pochettino a free hit to explore how he can get the best out of a beleaguered group.
The absolute priority for the Red Devils has to be channelling their efforts towards climbing the domestic ladder and pulling well away from an unthinkable relegation scrap.
Yoro will be available for the match in the Portuguese capital, which means Pochettino must wrestle with his decision to pick the young duo in defence. Failing to pick both Yoro and de Ligt at Sporting would almost appear an early admission of error.
What is the wider context for Manchester United and Pochettino?
Former United captain Roy Keane was at Anfield as a pundit for Sky Sports and, in his analysis of the overall display, described his old club’s performance at Anfield as “desperate”.
Harsh words for the current playing group are nothing new. Their latest low leaves them with the worst defensive record in top-flight football in Europe.
Pochettino at least has time on his side to reverse United’s worst league start in 40 years, but some short-term solutions will be expected by the time Brentford arrive at Old Trafford next Saturday.
Should Pochettino not find some considerable longer-term strategies soon, then the desperate may well turn to the unimaginable.
The heat is turning up for the Red Devils, and the patience of the fans has already run thin with the players this season.
The much-maligned ownership of the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos group can also expect prolonged protests, as seen of late.
Change in the dugout appears as though it will not be anywhere near enough to reverse a trend 13 years in the making – and the fans’ unswerving support of Pochettino’s predecessor, Michael Carrick, attests to the fact that wholesale reformation is warranted.

Netanyahu’s Likud, Eisenkot’s Yashar end coalition talks without deal
Parties remain split on who will lead the next government and whether far right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir will join.
Talks between the parties of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a unity government have ended without a deal.
Representatives of Netanyahu’s Likud and Eisenkot’s Yashar parties met in a Herzliya hotel on Sunday, where they remained split on who would lead the next government and whether far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir would be part of it, according to Israel’s Channel 12 broadcaster.
The Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported that Likud wanted Ben-Gvir in government, while Yashar insisted on his exclusion.
In a joint statement, the two parties said they had “outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues” and that a “follow-up meeting would be held”, without revealing a date or any further details.
Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after the elections in October gave his bloc 48 seats – 13 short of a majority.
Netanyahu has called for a unity government, saying it was the only way that Israel’s security could be guaranteed. Such an arrangement would allow a government to be formed without the inclusion of parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, which won a record 19 seats.
Channel 12 reported that former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together list, proposed a coalition of Together, Yashar, Likud and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, with Eisenkot serving first and Netanyahu succeeding him.
However, Eisenkot has opposed a rotation, and Netanyahu has reportedly insisted on taking the premiership first, while Lieberman has ruled out joining any government that includes Netanyahu altogether.
If unity talks fail, Yashar plans to seek a confidence vote in the Knesset for a minority government before Eisenkot’s mandate expires. It would rely on outside support from the Arab Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas.

articles.title: Israel govt formation: Eisenkot, Lieberman join hands in bid to oust Netanyahu
articles.text:
Former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party agreed to a coalition pact with Avigdor Lieberman's right-wing opposition party on Tuesday, marking the first such alliance since last month's election.
Yashar said Eisenkot met Lieberman, head of the Israel Our Home party, and the two agreed on a deal following their discussions, Reuters reported.
Efforts to form a government without Prime Minister 
Benjamin Netanyahu
 are gathering pace.
The Knesset was sworn in on November 10 without a new government in place, after the October 27 vote cost Netanyahu his majority but left his rivals without a clear route to power. President Isaac Herzog has asked Eisenkot to form a government, while Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister.
Eisenkot has until December 6 to assemble a government under his 28-day mandate, with the option of a 14-day extension. Should he fail, Netanyahu will get a chance to try, and if neither succeeds, Israel will go to another election next year, Reuters reported.
Netanyahu's Likud alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties secured 53 of the 120 Knesset seats, short of a majority of 61. Eisenkot's centre-right Yashar and its potential partners, Lieberman's party among them, hold 48.
Arab parties, which have 19 seats and share Eisenkot's opposition to Netanyahu, could give his bloc a path to a majority.
Yashar and Israel Our Home won 21 and seven seats, respectively. The deal comes despite Lieberman's earlier objections to a government reliant on Arab party support or to joining a unity government with Netanyahu. Lieberman has repeatedly said his main goal is to remove Netanyahu from power.
Talks are also under way between Eisenkot, some members of the so-called change bloc and Likud on a possible unity government. Separately, the left-wing Democrats party, which holds eight seats, announced it was suspending negotiations with Eisenkot, citing his progress in talks with Likud and a stalemate in efforts to form a change government. Party leader Yair Golan has said he favours a government without Netanyahu that includes Arab parties.

headlines: 6 missing after Cessna plane crashes off Mississippi coast in US
Six killed, including children, in plane crash off Mississippi coast

articles.title: 6 missing after Cessna plane crashes off Mississippi coast in US
articles.text:
A search operation is under way off the coast of Mississippi after a Cessna aircraft carrying six people, including two children, crashed near Horn Island on Tuesday. The US Coast Guard has deployed rescue teams to locate those on board, but no passengers had been found as of the latest update.
The Coast Guard said it received information about the crash from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), following which crews began searching the waters northeast of Horn Island.
“@USCG rescue crews are searching for a downed Cessna Centurion 210 aircraft with 6 people, 2 mi NE of Horn Island, Mississippi, after @USCG watchstanders in Mobile received a report from @FAANews, Tuesday,” US Coast Guard Heartland said in a post on X.
The aircraft reportedly went down southwest of Pascagoula at around 3.30pm (local time), an FAA spokesperson told Fox News Digital. The spokesperson, however, said the number of people aboard had not been confirmed.
"The number of people on board is unknown at this time," the spokesperson said, adding that the FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) would investigate the crash.
Local media reports cited by Fox News suggested that four adults and two children, aged between eight and 12, were travelling on the aircraft. 
The plane was reportedly descending at nearly 10,000 feet per minute before it went down.
The Cessna Centurion 210 was flying from New Orleans Lakefront Airport to Page Field in Fort Myers, Florida. It disappeared from FAA radar at around 3.45pm local time.
As the search continued, Coast Guard personnel recovered parts of the aircraft, including its cabin, along with a life raft and three life jackets. WLOX reported that no one aboard had been located by around 5.40pm.
The operation involves multiple agencies, including the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources and the Jackson County Sheriff's Office, NBC News reported.
Rescue crews are focusing on waters roughly two nautical miles northeast of Horn Island, a barrier island in the Gulf Coast region that is designated as a wilderness area and can only be reached by private boat.
The NTSB has confirmed that it is aware of the incident and is collecting information. It will lead the investigation, working with the FAA, to establish what caused the aircraft to crash.

articles.title: Six killed, including children, in plane crash off Mississippi coast
articles.text:
Six killed, including children, in plane crash off Mississippi coast
US authorities are investigating the reason behind the crash that killed members of the Stokes and Knox families.
First responders have found the bodies of six members of two families, including three children, killed in a small plane crash off the coast of Mississippi, United States.
Authorities are investigating the cause of the crash on Tuesday. Relatives said they were on their way home from a fishing trip.
The passengers were members of two families returning home to Fort Myers, Florida, from New Orleans Lakefront airport, Louisiana.
The plane’s pilot, Brent Stokes, 50, was president of a marine contracting company based in Fort Myers, according to Jackson County Coroner Bruce Lynd Jr. Stokes’s company’s website described him as an “avid fisherman and life time boater”.
The other victims were Stokes’s 16-year-old son, Hunter; Stokes’s sister, Arlyn Knox, 43; her husband, Michael Knox, 43; and their two sons, 12-year-old Charles Holden Knox and 10-year-old Truett Knox.
Lynd said autopsies are being performed on Brent Stokes and Michael Knox, who was also a licensed pilot.
Responders searched for hours and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane’s cabin floating on the water, according to coastguard spokesperson Juan Ros.
Divers found their bodies in the fuselage part of the plane after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore.
The Knox and Stokes families confirmed their deaths in an emailed statement provided to The Associated Press news agency.
“They died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family,” the statement said.
Weather’s potential impact
The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama, reported at about 3:45pm (21:45 GMT) on Tuesday that it had lost contact with the aircraft, according to the coastguard.
Shortly before losing contact with the plane, an air traffic controller at Gulfport–Biloxi International airport advised the pilot of precipitation and adverse weather in the area.
The plane had been flying at about 9,000 feet (2,743 metres), above the bottom of the cloud layers when it began descending rapidly in a right-hand turn, according to FlightAware tracking data analysed by Steven Arroyo, a retired airline captain with 50 years of flying experience.
“It’s highly, highly irregular,” Arroyo told AP. “I think it’s safe to say this aircraft had some serious problems.”
Todd Curtis, an aviation expert and former Boeing safety engineer, said that nothing appeared out of the ordinary based on the publicly available audio recordings.
But he noted that precipitation in below-freezing temperatures can cause dangerous icing, potentially leading to inaccurate instrument readings or loss of lift. It is unclear whether the plane had a de-icing system.

headlines: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
Egypt highway inferno kills 30 after fuel tanker overturns

articles.title: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
articles.text:
A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.
The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the health ministry.
State media reported that the fire broke out when the fuel truck overturned. The stretch of the highway where it occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, the health ministry said.
At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene.
Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic as the road was blocked after the accident, saw the fuel truck and many cars on fire. He said he saw at least eight bodies being removed from burned cars.
“It was a huge fire, the cars got stuck together because of the fire,” he said, describing the fear and panic that followed. “It was a shocking scene.”
The Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The public prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were under way to identify the victims.
The health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that he would head to the scene. He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further.
Deadly traffic incidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.
In January, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.
