headlines: Kilmar Ábrego García, man at center of Trump deportation battle, leaves US
Kilmar Ábrego García, target of Trump’s immigration crackdown, lands in Spain after ‘leaving happy’

articles.title: Kilmar Ábrego García, man at center of Trump deportation battle, leaves US
articles.text:
Kilmar Ábrego García has left the United States of his own volition, his lawyers confirmed on Tuesday, with the Department of Homeland Security confirming that he was travelling to Spain.
A source close to Ábrego said Madrid was his first stop but that it would not be his final destination.
The Salvadorian immigrant was at the center of a months-long legal battle since he was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 by the Trump administration, in defiance of a court’s protection. He was held in Cecot, a notorious mega-prison.
He was ultimately returned to the US after a decision by the supreme court three months later. Since then, Ábrego has been fighting a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials.
The Washington Post reported earlier on Tuesday that he negotiated a deal with federal authorities to depart the US voluntarily in order to avoid being forcibly removed.
In a statement, the US senator Chris Van Hollen, who has advocated for Maryland resident Ábrego and who met with him in El Salvador last year, described him as a “free man” and referenced Ábrego’s agreement with the Trump administration.
“While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said. “I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution.”
The 31-year-old has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the US illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.
He was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadorian prison in what an official later called an “administrative error”. Facing public pressure and a court order, the Trump administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the justice department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Ábrego for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.
The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and, most recently, Liberia.
“We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department,” one of Ábrego’s attorneys, Sean Hecker, said in a statement provided to the Washington Post. “He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”
Additional reporting by Ashifa Kassam in Madrid and the Associated Press

articles.title: Kilmar Ábrego García, target of Trump’s immigration crackdown, lands in Spain after ‘leaving happy’
articles.text:
Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadorian national whose mistaken deportation turned him into a symbol of Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts, has landed in Spain.
Ábrego García arrived in Madrid on Wednesday after leaving the United States of his own volition.
“I feel free of everything evil that has followed me up until this point,” he told reporters on a video call just hours after he touched down. “I’m happy … because this time I’m leaving with my freedom, not like before when they took me out inhumanely.”
He added: “The government does not decide where my story continues. My family and I will decide our future.”
Prior to his departure, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents met him at the airport and removed his ankle monitor, according to We Are Casa, a Maryland-based advocacy group.
As he made his way through the Madrid airport, Ábrego García did not speak to reporters, instead raising his fist in the air as he climbed into a waiting van.
Ábrego García became a lightning rod in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in 2025 after he was deported to El Salvador in what an official later called an “administrative error”.
The 31-year-old had been living in the US since 2019, after a judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador due to the dangers posed by a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under ICE supervision, but he was not given residency status.
Married to an American woman, the Maryland resident was part of a group of more than 200 people sent by the US to Cecot, a notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison, in violation of the US immigration judge’s 2019 order.
Amid public outcry, he was returned to the US after a decision by the supreme court. Since then, Ábrego García has been fighting government efforts to deport him for a second time to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.
On Wednesday, his lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said the Trump administration had wanted to deport Ábrego García “handcuffed, on an ICE flight bound for Liberia” on Tuesday.
“And what happened? He walked out a free man, without any restrictions, without shackles on his feet. He left for the country of his choosing, and he did so on a commercial flight, alongside everyone else,” Sandoval-Moshenberg added.
He described it as a “complete victory”, adding: “Instead of flying ICE Air, he flew United Airlines. Instead of being in shackles, he was in economy plus.”
He said Ábrego García had negotiated a deal with federal authorities in which they had agreed to allow him to leave the country, removing obstacles such as the ankle monitor and taking him off the no-fly list, as long as he left by 24 November. The Department of Homeland Security said on Tuesday Ábrego García had “self-deported” to Spain.
Sandoval-Moshenberg described Ábrego García’s departure from the US as temporary, saying that he would decide where to settle for the next two years as he waited out the remainder of the Trump administration.
“Mr Ábrego García has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a US citizen spouse and the father of a US citizen child,” he said. “We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritise reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland.”
On Wednesday, Ábrego García’s lawyer, Chris Newman, said his client had landed in Spain as a tourist and that he had no plans to meet with any politicians while in Spain. “I can confirm that he’s coming here with the intention of staying for just a few days and that he already has tickets, one could say, for his next appointment,” he told Spanish media.
His departure this week was celebrated by many who had sought to push back against the Trump administration’s pursuit of Ábrego García.
“They wanted to leave him there to rot for the rest of his life. Instead, we saw our judicial system work alongside a strong legal team to produce this outcome, where Kilmar Ábrego García is able to chart his own future,” said Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat who traveled to Cecot to visit Abrego Garcia in April last year.
Van Hollen, who is vying to become Senate majority leader when Democrats regain control of Congress next year, has made Ábrego García’s case and opposition to the administration’s sweeping deportation crackdown central to his vision for the party.
“Ábrego García’s journey is an example of our constitution working despite the attacks of the Trump administration,” Van Hollen added. He said he had spoken with the Spanish ambassador to the United States, Ángeles Moreno Bau, and briefed her on “all the wrongs that have been committed by the Trump administration against Kilmar Ábrego García”, adding that he was pleased Ábrego García was now in Spain and “able to continue telling his story”.

headlines: Trump tariff threat ‘unacceptable’, says Brazil, as China denounces levies as baseless
Brazil blasts ‘unacceptable’ new US tariff proposals

articles.title: Trump tariff threat ‘unacceptable’, says Brazil, as China denounces levies as baseless
articles.text:
Brazil has said it will not bend to the new US tariff “threat” and China accused Washington of “political manipulation” in the wake of Donald Trump’s latest economic salvo against 14 major trading partners.
Brazil’s government said on Wednesday: “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.
It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.
Brazil was particularly singled out for in the announcement after trade talks stalled. The Trump administration claimed on Wednesday that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries.
The new tariffs are being imposed under a law which allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base.”
The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.
China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. The US said China would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%. The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was a source of excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.
“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”
Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.
China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined,” said Derek Scissors, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”
Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.
It added it was “preparing and submitting rebuttal comments on the preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions and allegations made by interested parties.”
In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in any sector, adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.
Taiwan was also singled out for new tariffs, but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing 15% tariff rate.
Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech product which account for over 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.
Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, and Thailand.
Tokyo’s top government spokesman, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.
Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.
However Democratic Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.”
“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs,” Wyden added. “Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”
With Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: Brazil blasts ‘unacceptable’ new US tariff proposals
articles.text:
Brazil blasts ‘unacceptable’ new US tariff proposals
President Lula’s office says Brazil will not yield to threats and aims for a negotiated resolution.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has voiced outrage over new tariffs proposed by US President Donald Trump’s administration on Brazilian aircraft and sugar.
Brazil was not ruling out “reciprocal measures”, Lula’s office said in a statement on Wednesday after the US proposed a 10 percent tariff on finished aircraft made by Brazilian planemaker Embraer.
“The unilateral decision by the USTR [Office of the United States Trade Representative] is an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the statement continued.
Washington also plans to raise duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas to rectify what it calls “unreasonable” trade practices.
The new tariff rate would ensure that sugar from Brazil could not be shipped through third countries into the United States, the USTR’s office said.
The move is part of a broader wave of proposed tariffs targeting 14 major trading partners, including China and the European Union.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said his office was proposing changes to tariffs imposed in July after Brazil made “no meaningful progress” on the issues.
Greer said Washington remains open to talks.
Brasilia said it had been negotiating “in good faith” with Washington for more than a year and that the two sides had agreed to establish a working group on trade issues in August.
The president’s office said Brazil would continue to seek “a negotiated solution” without indicating whether the country would exercise its right to challenge the proposed tariffs before the World Trade Organization.
The tariffs, which could take effect as early as January, could raise the price US carriers pay for Embraer jets at a time when they are already grappling with a surge in jet fuel prices due to the US war on Iran.

headlines: Indian Cockroach movement leader asks court for permission to fly to UK
Leader of India’s Cockroach movement says he was stopped from boarding flight to UK

articles.title: Indian Cockroach movement leader asks court for permission to fly to UK
articles.text:
A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi high court to give him permission to fly to the UK after immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him boarding a flight early on Tuesday morning.
The court is scheduled to hear Saurav Das’s case on Thursday morning. His lawyer asked the court for a quick hearing because Das has by now already missed some of his engagements at British universities and can only attend the other events on his itinerary if he is allowed to fly out as soon as possible.
Das, 27, is one of the main faces of the Cockroach movement, which shot into the political firmament out of nowhere in May to challenge the Narendra Modi government with street protests.
The movement succeeded in forcing the education minister to resign in July over exam leaks and has since functioned as a pressure group.
Das had been invited by the Oxford Union Society to participate in a “fireside chat” on the movement.
Indian student groups at Edinburgh, Cambridge, Queen Mary University of London and the London School of Economics have also invited him to speak.
“Students want to know how we succeeded without any violence, how we began and where we are going. There is a great curiosity about the movement,” Das told the Guardian.
Reports in the Indian media have alleged that Das was informed well before the flight that his passport contained discrepancies.
“None of these reports is true,” said Das. “I received an email five hours before my flight saying that I should not use my passport for travel. It gave no reason. And I did not see the email until I arrived at Delhi airport. What’s more, I’ve travelled abroad before on this passport since it was issued in 2019 so what’s the problem with it now?”
He suspects that the government is using a frivolous case filed in Chennai against him as a pretext. The case has been filed, Das surmises, by someone hostile to the Cockroach movement and disputes his citizenship.
Das believes he was deliberately stopped by a government that is “scared” of someone such as him speaking abroad about the ideals of Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru (independent India’s first prime minister) and that it wanted to make an example of him.
“It’s a chilling signal to young Indians that we can do what we like, that if we can do this to a leader of a movement, we can do this to you too,” said Das.
In recent years, the government has stopped foreign speakers and academics, including several from the UK, from entering India.
Last year, Francesca Orsini, a professor at Soas University of London, was stopped at Delhi airport and deported despite holding a valid visa. The government said she had been blacklisted for allegedly conducting research and speaking at events while visiting on a tourist visa in 2024.
Also last year, Nitasha Kaul, a professor at Westminster University, was detained at Bangalore airport and deported for “anti-India activities”.
Some people who find themselves blacklisted have chosen to fight back. In 2023, the UK-based journalist Amrit Wilson had her overseas citizen of India card which allows free movement into India cancelled, also for alleged “anti-India activities”.
She took legal action and earlier this week, the Delhi high court ruled that the government had failed to give any concrete details of what it meant by “anti-India activities”.
The court has given the government a week to issue a fresh notice, this time giving specific reasons.

articles.title: Leader of India’s Cockroach movement says he was stopped from boarding flight to UK
articles.text:
A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has said he was prevented from leaving Delhi to fly to the UK to give talks on the viral group’s protests.
Saurav Das, 27, has been at the forefront of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which has amassed millions of social media followers since its launch in May. Das, who was due to fly out early on Tuesday, said immigration officials told him at the airport that his passport had been flagged.
The incident comes a month after he was detained for defying a security crackdown in Delhi during protests demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner.
“This coward government did not allow me to board my flight to London where I was invited by prestigious universities like Oxford, Cambridge, LSE (London School of Economics), Edinburgh to deliver talks on the Cockroach movement,” Das said in a social media post late on Monday. “Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual government was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions.”
Das was due to speak at the Oxford Union society on 1 December.
CJP-organised protests in July over alleged examination irregularities forced the education minister to resign, marking a rare climbdown by the government of Narendra Modi.
Critics say human rights and press freedoms have declined since Modi came to power in 2014. Earlier this month, India barred more than 100 foreign speakers from attending a democracy summit organised by the opposition Congress party. Those denied visas included a Norwegian journalist who had previously questioned Modi about press freedom.
In 2022, authorities prevented Sanna Irshad Mattoo, an award-winning photographer from India-administered Kashmir, from flying to the US to collect her Pulitzer prize.

Trouble for Netanyahu? Israeli judges question key charges in corruption trial

Judges recommend prosecutors end corruption case against Netanyahu

articles.title: Trouble for Netanyahu? Israeli judges question key charges in corruption trial
articles.text:
Israeli judges on Wednesday urged prosecutors to reconsider three corruption cases against prime minister 
Benjamin Netanyahu
. The judge stated that the chances of convicting him in one bribery case were low and questioned whether an offence had been committed in another, in a major setback for the long-running prosecution.
The judges at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, who has the authority to decide whether the cases should proceed, and asked her to consider dropping one of the charges and reassessing the others.
The panel said there was little likelihood of a conviction in Case 4,000, which alleges that Netanyahu granted regulatory favours to a telecommunications mogul in exchange for favourable coverage on a news website. The judges also expressed serious doubts over whether the alleged conduct in Case 2,000, involving a proposed deal with a newspaper publisher, amounted to a criminal offence.
They left open the possibility of a conviction in Case 1,000, in which Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust for accepting gifts from wealthy businessmen in return for helping them with their interests.
Baharav-Miara told the court that she and her team would consider the judges’ recommendations and remain open to all options based on the evidence, according to a transcript provided by a Justice Ministry spokeswoman to New York Times.
The judges stressed that their remarks reflected their assessment of the evidence at this stage and did not amount to a verdict.
Netanyahu, who has denied all wrongdoing and described the prosecution as a political witch hunt, said the trial had collapsed and called for it to end immediately.
“Today, the trial has fallen,” he said in a televised statement, describing the judges’ comments as “a ray of truth and justice”.
The prime minister said it had taken 10 years for the truth to emerge, referring to the investigations into his conduct that began about a decade ago. He also spoke of the “terrible suffering” endured by him and his family.
Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate but interlocking cases. Prosecutors allege that he granted government and regulatory benefits to business figures in exchange for gifts and favourable media coverage for him and his family.
Three cases at the centre of trial
In Case 4,000, Netanyahu is accused of helping the controlling shareholder of Israel’s largest telecommunications company, Bezeq, in return for positive coverage on the news website Walla, which the businessman owned. The judges said the chances of conviction in the bribery case were low enough to warrant reconsideration.
Case 2,000 concerns an alleged backroom arrangement between Netanyahu and the owner of a popular daily newspaper. The proposed deal, which never came to fruition, would have involved favourable coverage of Netanyahu in exchange for measures against a rival publication. The judges said they had serious doubts that the evidence established a criminal offence.
Case 1,000 involves allegations that Netanyahu accepted nearly $300,000 in gifts, including cigars and champagne, from Hollywood producer Arnon Milchan and Australian billionaire James Packer between 2007 and 2016.
Prosecutors allege that Netanyahu sought to help Milchan extend a tax exemption and used his influence to assist him in renewing his US visa. The attorney general said the options in this case were either a verdict or a plea deal.
Netanyahu completed his testimony in June, prompting the judges to take stock of the proceedings, which have been delayed over the years, including by the war in Gaza.
Political future in the balance
The development comes at a crucial moment for Netanyahu, whose political future has been thrown into uncertainty after last month’s election failed to produce a clear parliamentary majority.
His rival, former military chief and centrist Gadi Eisenkot, has been given the first opportunity by Israel’s president to form a new government. Netanyahu and his allies won more seats than Eisenkot’s bloc but fell short of securing an outright majority.
Netanyahu’s indictment and trial have contributed to years of political instability in Israel, with several mainstream parties refusing to join coalitions led by him, arguing that he is unfit to govern while facing criminal charges.
The judges’ intervention could now give Netanyahu a significant political boost, though the cases remain before the court and no final decision has been made on whether they will be dropped or proceed to judgment.

Two Syrian security personnel killed in ISIL suicide attack
Syrian forces say the attack in northeastern Syria’s city of Hasakah involved four assailants who were all killed.
A suicide attack by the ISIL (ISIS) group has killed two security personnel and wounded five others in Syria’s northeastern city of Hasakah, according to local authorities.
Four gunmen targeted an Internal Security Forces (ISF) checkpoint on Wednesday in the Mushirfa neighbourhood of Hasakah, an official statement from the governorate’s media directorate said.
All four of the assailants died in the attack, two in clashes with security forces and the other two in suicide explosions, the ISF said.
One of the suicide attackers, Syrian media reported, was riding a booby-trapped motorcycle when he detonated himself at the entrance of the post.
The deputy governor of Hasakah, Ahmed al-Hilali, vowed “to uncover the circumstances of the attack and identify the perpetrators”.
“Ensuring the safety of citizens and the stability of the region is a responsibility from which we will not waver,” al-Hilali added.
The ISF shared photos from the site on their X page, including an image of the vest they say was worn by one of the two perpetrators who was “neutralised” by the forces.
Continued attacks
A report in February by the UN said that Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and two of his senior cabinet ministers were the targets of five foiled assassination attempts by ISIL over the past year.
The report did not provide specific dates as to when the foiled attacks took place, though it noted their locations in northern Aleppo, the country’s most populous province, and the southern province of Deraa.
In October, the Interior Ministry reported that two members of Syria’s internal security forces were killed and five wounded in clashes with a suspected ISIL cell during a raid on the outskirts of Damascus.
